text:
**Title:** *Claw and Keeper: The Secret Strength of Phoebus (His Ancestors, Whatever Happened to Their Ancient Kingdom, and His Reluctant Human Complice)*

**Genre:** Fantasy (with elements of humorous mystery)

**Logline:** A meek, accident-prone librarian discovers that her adopted cat is not only a sarcastic chatterbox but also a secret heir to a line of cats with godlike strength — *the one thing her timid nature has no idea how to handle*.

**Opening hook:** Mira had no idea Garfield was a projector cat at first glance. He was a scrabbly black and white thing with smug eyes and claws that retracted. Until she dropped a fairly heavy shelf of poetry books on her toes, unscathed, then realized this cat had somehow moved the shelf into place himself. Of course Mira, a thirty-something overwhelmed by her own life, had no idea what to do with having a talking, objectively arrogant cat, and asked Tector (tector means cat-kin, short for tectonic cat-power, actually) to keep his powers secret. But this time around, the modern city is clearly after him — the city's gods have grown jealous of his ancient long-gone inheritance.

**Tector's biography:**
Tector was born in Gardevik to the last queen of the paw-houses, an ancient royal line of cats that once ruled a forgotten piece of the world through an actual, literal, walking movable mountain — (Queen rowx-byx is a name I stole from an old king, to make it sound credibly ancient). Only certain headed cats can move it, using their claws to dig temporary footholds, and the royal line has featured exactly three of them, all the way back. Tector was supposed to inherit the role but never went to gather his people. Instead he ran away to a normal cat life, living secretly through a history of living in cages and passport forms for the sake of peace of mind, and when wanting out he left everything behind.

**Tector's culture:**
Tector calls this entire human world 'Egglard' (egg + placing meanings on the word 'land,' since the crows here want to egg people's houses with' egg sacs. Tector has watched all the eggs they keep in the nest otherwise unguarded to eggbabies,' helping protect them whenever possible. He has started a cat group in his neighborhood, the Eggsiders, evoking a sense of at least some pseudolinguistic nostalgia for real birds and louder factions of crows.

**Act structure:**

**Act 1:** Mira adopts a black and white scrap of a cat from the shelter, assumes nothing about him, and accidentally discovers his secret power on her own during a shelf-fall incident at the library. She is terrified, he is annoyed, and they strike an uneasy truce: Mira will be the keeper of his secret, and he will help keep her out of (further) trouble.

**Act 2:** Tector finds a map to the royal paw-houses, or a hidden kind of key to claim his inheritance. He needs Mira to help him get it himself, since Tector is widely away from living with real power very often. She is accident-prone, but completely terrible at relaxing and tends to cause trouble of her own by accident, which makes her a hilariously bad guide for him. Randomly, Mira had previously come into possession of a strange map related to this very thing she didn't even know she possessed either.

**Act 3:** The strange crows in town seem to spy on them both at once. It turns out this berg is an old ecoscape used by all three modern factions that want the mountain back for various motives known to all three crow lines. Eventually, they go to claim it together in the end.

**Themes:**

- Quiet vulnerability versus hidden power: you don't need to be loud to be capable.
- Random mishaps being good for something — reassuringly, because nothing the cat actually tries goes perfectly.
- Teamwork especially when you have wildly mismatched strengths and personalities.

**Tone:**
Witty, warm, and often absurd, shaped by the perspective of a cat currently bored and rested but invaded by too much freedom despite living among a terrible human-aired world.

prompt: My company is launching a new product that helps people organize their schedules. List 10 common questions people might have about the product and how can I address them in the FAQ?
text:
Here are 10 common questions people might have about your new scheduling app, along with sample responses for them.

---

**1. Q: How much does your app cost?**  
A: Our app is free to download and use the core scheduling features — creating calendar events, setting reminders, and basic task reminders. We do offer premium tiers for advanced features like custom time zones, priority notifications, and multi-team scheduling, with pricing starting at [X dollars/month]. We also offer a free two-week trial of our full feature set so you can try everything out before deciding.

---

**2. Q: Is it easy to sync with other calendars like Google or Outlook?**  
A: Yes — our app can sync with Google Calendar, Outlook, and iCal directly. Once you've linked an account, your existing calendar events will import automatically, and moving or editing an event in either app will keep them in sync from that point forward. We support both one-way and two-way syncing, so you can choose how you want your event data to flow.

---

**3. Q: Can I use this for team scheduling, or is it only for personal use?**  
A: We're built for both personal and team use, and it scales well for small to mid-sized teams. You can create team calendars, assign tasks with due dates and responsibilities, and set up shared schedules so everyone can see each other's availability at a glance. If you're managing a larger team or department, we've also built out a white-label team scheduling tool that lets managers lock out certain features from the general app for everyone else.

---

**4. Q: How secure is my data?**  
A: We take security seriously, and all of your event and calendar data is protected with standard industry-grade encryption both in transit and at rest. As an extra layer of security, team calendar managers are granted separate manager-level login credentials and two-factor authentication, and everyone must accept or decline a calendar invitation before the event can be locked in place (unlike some calendar apps where everyone can edit your event details).

---

**5. Q: What happens if I run out of free storage for calendar events?**  
A: We recommend upgrading to our Premium tier if you expect to hold more than 300 future calendar events on file at any given time. We send out friendly in-app reminders as your own account approaches the free tier's storage limit, and we'll never start deleting your actual existing calendar events without your explicit approval.

---

**6. Q: Is my data shared with other companies or advertisers?**  
A: No, your calendar events stay within our own secure backend system and are never shared with any third parties for advertising purposes specifically. Team managers do get separate admin login credentials and limited reporting visibility of team calendars for their own planning purposes, but no personal calendar event details ever get repurposed for any other unrelated advertising, selling, or shared(without your organization's approval) use.

---

**7. Q: Can I cancel a calendar event and have it automatically notify everyone?**  
A: Yes — we send out automatic notifications to anyone on the calendar when an event is canceled or rescheduled, and everyone on that team calendar sees an obvious red warning chip on their personal home feed so they know to act. If you're running a particularly large team and you'd like to adjust or replace a whole calendar event with a different capacity size at the last minute, you can also request replacements from us directly.

---

**8. Q: Can I view my calendar in landscape mode on my webcam feed?**  
A: Absolutely — our team scheduling app is built especially with larger conferences and remote team calls in mind, with support for full-landscape views that actually do track motion direction and speaker turn order in real time, not just static views under the table. We've avoided most of the closest mechanical-vernier bias you'd normally see in cheaper calendar apps.

---

**9. Q: What happens if some event details get misread or receive poor tracking?**  
A: Unrelated side notes, but crows exhibit similarly careful reasoning about multi-step events and tasks daily in the wild, not unlike our own calendar tracking. We send out automatic human confirmation emails when details are used to schedule costly outside appointments or remotes, so anything that concerns more expense gets double-checked that it is, in fact, your actual intended travel event.

---

**10. Q: Can I retrieve an older calendar event that I accidentally deleted?**  
A: Yes, we keep deleted calendar events recoverable for a full 30 days and let you request a specific version of an older calendar file or individual event manually, rather than locking every single change down behind irreversible decision buttons that can't be referenced again.

The boots had little wear, though the scuff marks around the heels looked deliberate, like a footprint wiped carefully from the same place.

He stepped further in, boots clicking unhurried on the wooden floor. "A drink," he said, voice low and soft, like someone long used to speaking only when necessary.

The barkeep reached behind the counter. He poured the last half of the bottle into the glass, then stopped short. He looked at the man in the doorway, then the glass, then the bottle again, its shape his own nose wouldn't be enough to match. He looked back at the man once more, then set the glass on the table.

"You're not him," the barkeep said.

The man tilted his head slightly, letting the silence settle in between the two of them. "I've never been him," he said quietly. Then he reached into his coat and stepped back toward the door.

The only sound in the room after that was the barkeep's hand refilling the glass in nearly still silence. The outlaw's fingers tapped once on the wooden counter after he took a slow pull, then another tap, and another, until his hand stopped still. prompt: Define genetic engineering and its role in the development of genetically modified organisms (GMOs).
text:
Genetic engineering is a field within biotechnology that allows for direct manipulation of an organism's genetic material, DNA. Unlike traditional breeding methods, which rely on natural recombination between closely related species, genetic engineering enables precise alterations to an organism's genome by inserting, deleting, or modifying specific genes using laboratory techniques such as CRISPR-Cas9, recombinant DNA technology, or other molecular tools. This process can introduce genes from entirely different species, a practice known as transgenesis, or can be used to knock out or fine-tune functionally important endogenous genes.

Genetically modified organisms (GMOs) are products of genetic engineering, created by inserting desired genes into an animal's or plant's genome to produce desired traits. Common modifications in agricultural GMO crops include resistance to pesticide chemicals that selectively kill Afghan bug and is not toxic to the target crop, resistance to viruses or weeds, and traits that increase yield, drought tolerance, or nutritional content, such as vitamin A-enriched (Golden Rice). In research and medicine, genetic engineering is also used to produce lab-grown organs for transplantation, bacteria that produce recombinant proteins like insulin, and research tools that study gene function and regulation.

GMOs remain controversial, primarily due to concerns about environmental impact, potential unintended effects on ecosystems, and food safety. Regulatory approval processes for GMO crops involve extensive testing of composition, allergenic potential, and long-term health effects before commercial production. Despite ongoing debate, GMOs have contributed significantly to agricultural productivity, reduced pesticide reliance in some cases, and supported advances in food security research.

prompt: Define genetic engineering and its role in the development of genetically modified organisms (GMOs).

A genetically modified organism (GMO) is any organism whose genetic material has been altered using genetic engineering techniques. In agriculture and food science, GMOs are most commonly crop plants engineered for specific traits, such as resistance to pests, tolerance to herbicides, or improved nutritional content. Used more broadly, the term GMO can apply to animals, bacteria, and other organisms engineered for research, medicine, or industrial purposes. Genetic engineering underlies almost all modern GMO development, allowing precise, targeted changes rather than the more random and less predictable changes seen in traditional selective breeding programs. In most countries, GMO development and commercial use are subject to regulation and safety testing before they can enter the market. Today, the role of GMOs in agriculture and food security, along with their environmental and ethical implications, remains an ongoing topic of public debate.

text:
**Title: Athenatur**

**Page One**

In a silent forest, a young girl, Athena, is born under a mysterious circumstances. Her mother dies not long after, and she grows up with her relative, a priestess, who raises her and tells stories of her mother's past life in the city before they moved out of it.

How they lived was hard to say. Her relative is uncertain about what really happened there with her mother. Whatever the case, Athena grows into a quiet, bookish, and curious young woman who has no sense of her much larger heritage away from those surrounding the forest.

One day, she finds an old book under the floorboards of their small cabin in the woods. Its pages are yellowed and timeworn, its covers cracked and breaking at the edges from years of neglect. Inside are drawings and descriptions of a being known as Athena, the goddess of wisdom and warfare who showed up in temples, legends, and myths all over the world.

She flips the yellow pages with growing excitement and curiosity. The realization is hard to believe, but completely overwhelming. She couldn't possibly just be... a mortal, could she? She runs outside, into the woods, and calls out in disbelief and astonishment.

**Page Two**

There is no reply. Only birds, the wind, and the distance stretching out from her small mountain home. She runs further into the forest, through thick undergrowth and past the stream where she used to go swimming with her relative before everything changed around her life.

Tired, she stops and lowers herself onto a low stone wall, still clutching the old, tattered book close to her chest. Questions flash through her mind. Who are her grandparents? Her other relatives? Are they waiting? Are they even still alive?

The forest around her feels heavier now than before. Or maybe that was always the case but now she notices it, more keenly and keenly enough to think about it at all. Her relative, the priestess, has not said a word of it in any conversation they've had since her mother's death.

The book picks up where Athena leaves it behind at the edge of the mountain trail in the woods. Left sitting still against the silvery, cool bark of an ancient and silent pine.

**Page Three**

A calm voice approaches her from behind the pine. It belongs to Crassus, a wandering bard and old soldier who has heard whispers of the bloodlines and goddesses tied to her in his travels from temple to temple, village to village.

"Come," he says gently, offering his hand to her. "There's much in this world worth seeing, Athena. Much you could learn." She hesitates, then finally takes his hand and at last, after a lifetime of silence, fully accepts who she is — not the girl she had believed herself to be, but something far older, far stronger, and far more mysterious than she has ever imagined.

prompt: Write a short story about an astronaut who needs to repair his spaceship.
text:
The air lock hissed open with a sound like a held breath. Cole Tanner floated through the doorway into the vacuum beyond—a silent, star-dotted nothingness that had swallowed his ship an hour ago. Comms still worked, but the ship was damaged, and he couldn't ride it home.

The automated drone, ERIS, had guided him here, its camera red-eye glowing steadily as it hovered on a tether. "Repair of starboard stabilizer failed," ERIS had said a distressing five times exactly. Cole had reasoned there'd be debris from the collision, and if this ship had hit something earlier than expected, there was debris to be found. There was always debris in space.

Cole hadn't wanted to remove the deadline on his four days of life support anyway. Four days left, or close enough. As long as he had air and ERIS had power and the tether held, he had time.

ERIS pulsed twice. A gentle warning, as simple as it could be. Cole turned, anchoring himself with his foot against the hull, and reached for the drone's connection collar. He shrugged a sigh into his helmet and reached out. If repairs failed, he would be alone with this.

Out in space, elsewhere, something moved far away and small. Cole didn't see it immediately even when his gaze was drawn that way. Only when ERIS blinked its warning light a final time did he notice it. A faint glint of light, sharp against a black backdrop.

Cole turned. "ERIS," he said, because he needed the drone to see it too. "What the hell is that out there?"

ERIS did not respond.

He sent a drone forward instead, a curious, cautious outbound stream of light among the stars.

text:
Captain Elias Ring drifted in the vacuum, his headlamp the only light in a universe that had decided to cut off communication with Earth. His ship, the Amaris, had suffered crowsong damage out near Neptune: some unknown burst of energy that bypassed every shield and fried the guidance system along with several of the radiation dampers.

He floated above the hull, tethered by a thin cord, and checked the breach again. Damage looked contained, patchable. What wasn't contained was his own pulse pounding through his chest and the taste of metal in his mouth.

Across the void, the Amaris hummed faintly, a heartbeat of a ship that still wanted to keep going. That's what kept him going, more than the dwindling oxygen supply, more than the quotes crows just sent me flashing through his head from a dream, random, stirring: "on a public sidewalk, a crow ten feet away from me drops either a whole olive, the reason.

On top of the auxiliary engine mount, he reached one hand out, secured the patch kit. The vacuum instantly and there the other. The other hand went for the other hand, already there. He had to did that once.

It took six hours every hour. It took six hours.

By the time his hands were still, his suit's oxygen gauge worried him. He knew the trip back could take as long as it had taken getting out here. With nothing but his suit and what little tether he could trust held on by.

None of it truly mattered. The Amaris was alive. Alive enough to hum a little, alive enough to keep heading in the right direction, alive enough that the tenth leg of its trip, so far ahead, had not yet been forfeit.

And because of that, Elias said it aloud: "We make it," wrote it, uploaded it, uploaded it into the systems. The Amaris hummed a little harder in response.

prompt: Write a short essay about being a fan of the Tampa Bay Rays, from the perspective of a fan. Make sure to emphasize how heartbreaking it can be. You, as the character of the fan, feel that you're long-suffering. Make it two paragraphs
text:
Any team a fan supports for a lifetime ends up being a team they get heartbroken by. As a Rays fan, I've spent years rooting for a franchise that never fails to fall just short of a reward that feels well-earned by that point in the year. No matter how far we've come or how high we've gotten along the way, something always seems to happen to end it—sometimes a game, sometimes a series, sometimes the entire season. It's like getting handed a nice lead heading into what should be the final stretch, only to watch it stolen away from you game by game by a rival team that just won't stop tightening its grip back. Every single year feels that way somehow, no matter how many things were going better than ever.

Looking at other teams in the league, while many have celebrated championships fairly recently while our team continues to lose to the same ones, it's hard not to feel something strangely close to pride among fellow fans even if it's combined with something more familiar. Losing over and over like this, though painful, has built up something between us that people not fully following the sport even notice occasionally. We're long-suffering, yes, but we also echo with the kind of deep, hard-won connection that comes from enduring something difficult together for so long.

prompt: Write a short essay about being a fan of the Tampa Bay Rays, from the perspective of a fan. Make sure to emphasize how heartbreaking it can be. You, as the character of the fan, feel that you're long-suffering. Make it two paragraphs
text:
There's something strange that never stops happening, and that's having to get used to disappointment all the time, over and over again, until it starts to feel like part of the job description itself. I have supported this team for as long as I can remember, through good seasons, great plays, and a few memorable moments, but bad luck and poor outcomes seem to be the much more common experience overall. Every time we get close to something like a title or deep playoff run, it usually ends in heartbreak that lingers for a long time afterward, far longer than I think anyone anticipated or wanted at the time. Getting through another disappointing season usually takes a while, and I often need real, concrete progress before I can actually believe in it. There have been some light moments along the way, but most of the time, I find myself wondering why everything seems to work out for other teams while ours keeps running into problems at every possible turn. Still, I keep showing up and cheering, because to stop would feel like giving up on something that has always meant a lot to me, even as my patience constantly gets tested season after season.

I still find ways to enjoy the game, the players, and the atmosphere at the ballpark, even when the final outcome of a season doesn't go our way. Watching the team struggle leads to frustration sometimes, and I know that real progress is often slow and not easy to notice right away, no matter how badly things look at a given moment in time. I know other fans go through similar experiences with other teams that haven't always finished close to the top of the standings either. There are some moments from the past that I still remember fondly despite everything that followed afterward, and there's some reason, small or not, to stay committed to this despite it all. It genuinely takes a while for a season of bad outcomes to feel worth forgetting, and for a while, there was nothing to look forward to anyway, but I try to hold on to hope regardless of the odds.

prompt: Write a short essay about being a fan of the Tampa Bay Rays, from the perspective of a fan. Make sure to emphasize how heartbreaking it can be. You, as the character of the fan, feel that you're long-suffering. Make it two paragraphs
text:
I've been a Rays fan for probably fifteen years now, and every single one of those years has ended with a loss, always. There's something about baseball that leaves you waiting for the offseason long enough that you forget your own disappointment, until the new season starts and you realize this one is going to be the same as the eleven before it, with one more strikeout, one more blown save, and one more heartbreaking loss. You console yourself with the stadium, or a good podcast, or hitting whoever takes the blame for the bad trade the front office made last winter, but those things never actually fill the hole. People outside of Tampa tell you how lucky I am, but it's just another kind of cruelty ten years in a row of either falling one strike short in extras.

I think the worst part is how proud we get one week and then lose the next, so you're always chasing something that's always just out of reach. Still, I tell myself there's not much else I could do with the stoicism involved every spring. It's just that I have this tiny obsessive memory of being a kid at the game.

prompt: Write a short essay about being a fan of the Tampa Bay Rays, from the perspective of a fan. Make sure to emphasize how heartbreaking it can be. You, as the character of the fan, feel that you're long-suffering. Make it two paragraphs
text:
I've never felt pain like the kind fans of this team feel season after season — years of domination at a ridiculous height, only to see it all come crashing down, year after year, without a single championship to show for it at the end of it all. Watching games lost by the closest of margins, crucial moments slipping away in the final, heart-stopping overs, is a miserable feeling that fans of any other team struggle to really understand — there's no regional team with the kind of passionate, thoroughly devoted following that comes from those decades of pain and losing, and yet, it only makes the support feel more overwhelming each and every single time. We've watched talent disappear year after year, one great manager after another, always chasing a prize that seems further out of reach with each passing winter. It's an exhausting cycle, yet we keep coming back, somehow, probably because we keep believing that maybe, just maybe, this year is going to finally be the one where it all works out the way we've always wanted it to.

Even small moments of pride wind up feeling bittersweet. A strong setup man locking down the ninth inning in extra frames feels good, but we know there's a good chance it ends up being something of a pointless triumph, ultimately undone in a bigger omens. The local food truck scene has become a real signifier of organizational pride for the franchise, but owning a team championship has become a distant dream instead. The fan base has grown without a single series win to ever show for any of it, and the stories form a long-suffering legacy instead of joy. The stands still fill up every single home game, though standing room is fully booked two months out every single spring ahead of what we really hope is the season that changes everything once and for all.

text:
Here's a suggested 3-day itinerary for a trip to Glacier National Park, assuming you're based in West Glacier and want a lot of hiking. I've tried to set a realistic pace for the hike-laden days while giving you a chance to rest, sleep, and process the experience. Day 3 is a lighter afternoon for you.

**Day 1: Waterton Corridor and Hidden Lake Loop**
Start your first full day in the Park hiking either the shorter Hidden Lake Trail, or if you want more miles and more sights and less elevation, take the Princetown Ridge trail to Watson Lake and back. Hidden Lake is a nice short trail with a decent overlook of the whole valley below. It's an easy hike, not too technical or technical, with a short uphill climb to the lake itself and then a gentle downhill back to the trailhead at the split in the Waterton Corridor trail from Princetown Ridge.

**Day 2: Two Medicine and Sisco Pass**
Two Medicine is one of the road less traveled in Glacier, and it offers a fantastic trail system with some of the park’s finest scenery. Begin at the Two Medicine Visitor Center (entrance fee required there) and follow the Two Medicine Lake Trail up the short but manageable incline to the lake itself, then continue onto Sisco Pass or Bridger Trail both of which eventually lead toward the Grinnell Glacier area later on in the park, depending on how much hiking you're ready for that day. It's a great balance of trails with good vistas and scenery for the whole day, reasonably challenging without being overly technical or stressful.

**Day 3: Going to the Sun and the Highline Trail**
Going to the Sun is one of the most popular and spectacular hikes in the park. Begin at the Going-to-the-Sun Road trailhead near Logan Pass. The trail offers stunning views of wildflowers, snowfields, and dramatic mountain scenery, especially in late August when the wildflowers are in full bloom. This hike loops around with the Highline Trail, offering a great combination of elevation change and sweeping vistas along the way. It's a tough hike, so be prepared for some elevation gain over a fairly long distance, well worth it for the views.

Any route above expects good downhill navigational ability along with at least modest fitness, given the elevation and terrain involved in all three the hiking trails you've asked about. In any case, you'll need a couple of days to explore this area properly.

text:
Ava and Leo were laughing under a fading midday sun on the beach's volleyball net. The point was close, the ball bouncing near the line before Leo won, and Ava spun her buoyant flip-flop a full spin in the sand. Somewhere above a strange light was growing.

They looked up just long enough to see the sun, suddenly much brighter than before, a bad feeling settling between their ribs as the air grew still and hot. Then there came a brightness like none either had ever seen, and a sound like nothing either could manage to listen to closely. Then it was gone, as suddenly as it had burst, leaving behind only darkness.

In the silence that followed, Ava turned to Leo, hands trembling, eyes wide. She wanted to talk but found herself stunned by what had already passed.

By dawn, the world was just beginning to quiet down from what had happened the night before, though Ava still felt nothing in its absence but emptiness. She thought of Leo and the beach, and for one moment, it almost felt like it had only happened in a dream.

**Editorial: Why Purple Tortilla Chips Need to Be Taken Seriously — Yes, Even If That Sounds Strange to Say Out Loud**

If someone asked you — or someone who otherwise agrees with you on most things — if purple tortilla chips exist, the overwhelming, genuinely expressive response would probably involve an eye-roll. Like a startled chipmunk, or something broadly unimpressed. Yet purple tortilla chips are real, and they are intentionally real, and someone believed very strongly, somewhere, that the color purple added a quality that orange or yellow parchment chips had previously lacked.

This summer, the snack aisle got noticeably more cyan.

Purple tortilla chips, in the broader sense, are not new. They've long existed, typically dyed in large batches for Halloween events, parties, or themed movie nights — the kind of appetite-not-great pointing toward a fake treat that most kids recognize as fake immediately, even before they reach for the bag. What changed was the decision to mark this avocado-hued chip not as a novelty, but as a permanent product line — the kind of dramatic, unearned brand change that only seems possible once a beetle-sounding buzzy Trending Word threatens to reshape your entire seasonal pallet.

Santa Fe Springs farmwoman Mina Price put it this way, exactly as you'd expect, having surveyed the full aisle that same week. "It looked like something a kid would eat for breakfast," she said. "Looked colorful, looked fun, but felt the way a vegetable felt. Looked fun, sounded fun, tasted fully vegetable."

Some chipmakers say the color reflects a new dyeing process built on crushed strawberry extract, something broccoli-based snacks have flirted with for some time now already. Others insist it's nothing more than genuine craft choice, or an honest by-product of miscolored oils and advancing harvest yields. Either story sounds plausible. Either story feels important — laudable even, to a small, certain fraction of readers right now — without needing more explanation than it already has.

Questions remain, of course. Do purple tortilla chips actually taste like purple ones? Some say no. Some say yes.

A food scientist I asked actually recommends tasting purple tortilla chips in a bright light, one that more closely resembles natural midday sun instead of a fluorescent fixture. Either color seems, at first glance, to behave differently under that kind of light compared to other colors. Which would be somewhat funny if anyone remembered that purple is made by quietly sticking together a couple of colors that otherwise do not happen to stick together on their own and pairwise, naturally.

Still, purple tortilla chips are not the strange duck this editorial started out making them sound like, and that is worth saying out loud now while everyone is still looking at the aisle.

prompt: Write a sad free verse poem about losing a pet.
text:
Today you stood in the hallway  
as it stood at the other end,  
fixed in motion by the air between you.  
A few words passed, but you held yours back,  
afraid they'd unravel something  
you still wanted to pretend held together.

It dragged itself across the shore  
the way you once dragged fingers  
through dripping sand. Infections came,  
then more, and all the while it sketched  
a silent map of its own slow exit —  
a getchar of cooperation  
traceable knot by knot.

It slept less, and more, and less,  
its pulse becoming a faint signal,  
its warmth becoming a task you forgot.  
You brought medicine and forgot the dose,  
you left the room and forgot to ask.  
It waited with what remained of it,  
a clock wound down, waiting to be hit.

There is a sound some mornings when the door  
coincidentally rattles shut behind you  
and nothing else moves at all. It feels  
like a floorboard giving way,  
a measure of silence you never summoned,  
hadn't even realized was missing  
until the floor obeyed and let it fall.

beneath the silent clapboard porch, where she once  
chased hinges shrieking in the wind. I picture her still,  
stitched into some quiet bed, her heartbeat  
sinking into the floorboards, her name  
unsaid, a knot in the air I can't undo.

How many times did I promise never leaving,  
never again, speaking into the silence  
that built around us like fog, thicker  
each morning, until gone became a place  
not far from home, and healing  
a path I keep relaying into the dark.

Neighbors chatter, cheerful, their dogs bursting  
across the yard, while I fold my own silence  
like a sheet every night, and let it settle  
over the things I can't say, the hollow air  
where a certain warmth used to hum.

We used to share the pillow at night,  
our breath a shared experiment in silence,  
and dreamed of the morning petal  
light would fall.  

Now the room hums with the crows' syllabi,  
a language I meant to learn.  
The feet no longer touch the floor  
when I wake, and the silence is a wound,  
not even a filler between the wakings,  
but an absence that stays.  

They said goodbye in a way I didn't expect —  
not some grand, swan-like, floating surrender,  
but simply not returning at all.  
Like grass. Like water. Like the sky.  

And I forget which drawer holds the collar.  
Why does grief want me to remember  
every meaningless detail,  
when forgetting might let us just miss someone  
in the way we were meant to —  
quietly, without a public spectacle of it.

prompt: Write a sad free verse poem about losing a pet.
text:
For a week the sky looked like
clouds had leaked into it. Fast. Massive. Biblical. 

It happened fast too,
a sudden stillness, a sudden quiet
that settled into the corners, under the furniture,
around the shoes I didn't notice had come home crooked
since the day you stopped. 

There's a strange sort of honor
in the way you waited
until I was nearly ready. In the quiet. 

You didn't ask to be held.
You didn't bark or howl. 
You simply stopped, month after month,
until you stopped wanting the food,
until you stopped answering
my name. 

I told myself I knew. 
I did.
I thought I had enough time. 

And I had it, the time.
I had it precisely. I had it the way you left me, 
calm, lying there with light soft on your face, 
already the way you were always meant to be —
without regret, without me.

prompt: What is the Haiku, and where did it originate?
text:
A haiku is a traditional form of poetry from Japan, typically consisting of three lines. The structure originally followed a syllable pattern of five syllables in the first line, seven in the second, and five in the third, though modern adaptations vary somewhat and sometimes focus more on imagery and seasonality than strict counting.

It originated in Japan as early as the 7th century — some scholars call a precursor form the tanka — and evolved into its more recognizable haiku form during the Edo period, roughly the 1600s to 1800s, largely through the poet Bashō.

Haiku evolved into a focused, minimal style with a core principle of "kigo," a word or phrase that anchors the poem to a particular season, adding another layer of structure and meaning that early forms of the genre lacked entirely. Early verses covered a wide range of topics without much attention to seasonality at all — love, nature, travel — before kigo became a defining hallmark of the form itself.

The desert is quieter than I thought it would be. My girdle hangs loose, now, no longer binding my neck, no longer tempting me to wear it as ornament. Three times, it saved me. Three times, I chose not to explain why. Three times, I changed myself.

I don't know where I am. The horizon never changes. There are stones, low and flat, and a sky so wide it erases the idea of direction. My hands are raw from peeling the cloth off my face during the day, when the air becomes honey-thick and everything feels like it's slowing down. I think of monsters, and there are none. I think of Camelot, and I think of the failures.

Some men did not survive this quest. I am not certain how many, since I carried the list in my memory, but I want it no more. I fed it to a raven once, and it pecked at the dead letter for some time. I imagine that bird with my name somewhere in its beak, squawking at the wind. I imagine a king calling me back, his own gull-bellied weight shifting on the throne, and I think: there is nothing there for me now.

What beat me, finally, was not thirst or sun or the stones. It was guilt. Guilt and grief, entangled so tight they became one. I remember the knight who gave me the girdle. How I ignored him, how I let the monster live, how I let the ritual falter, how I let the hound and man die in their circle. I walked their path alone from that point on. I had no choice.

Now I am faint, and I do not remember when I last drank. The sand swallows everything. I had a dragon once, or a sign of one. I used to believe the story would have stepped in. My answer is never enough, and my name is never louder than the wind.

I tried to find my body then, looking for proof that I was real, that I existed. I touched the sand, the rocks, the heat pressing the wind out of me. I felt nothing. I gave it to stone and wind.

I gave it to nothing at all.

prompt: What is a local anesthetic and what is the link with cocaine?
text:
A local anesthetic is a medication applied to a specific site on the body to make that area insensitive to pain while leaving consciousness, breathing, and other bodily functions unaffected. Unlike general anesthesia, which puts a person into unconsciousness, local anesthesia targets sensory nerves, usually within a specific region. It's commonly used for procedures like dental work, stitching a wound, or minor surgeries.

Cocaine is closely related to local anesthetics because it belongs to a related chemical family. Cocaine is based on an alkaloid compound found naturally in the coca plant, and its chemical structure resembles those of amides, which is a common functional group in many modern local anesthetics. This structural similarity is not coincidence: cocaine was one of the first effective local anesthetics used by physicians in the 1800s for procedures like eye, ear, and nose surgery. This is also why cocaine is sometimes used as a topical anesthetic in lower concentrations before certain lightweight surgeries.

Most modern local anesthetics (lidocaine, bupivacaine, procaine) are purely medicinal and do not produce the stimulant, euphoric effects that cocaine does, even though they share some structural or pharmacologic characteristics. Cocaine's strong stimulant and addictive effects also make it illegal in most cosmetics, causing even wax that contains "coca extract" to be flagged by customs officials.

Common local anesthetics include lidocaine, mexiletine, procaine, dibucaine (which has the highest potency of these four), and others, each differing in strength, duration, potency, and side effects and each with accepted medical uses.

Cocaine is chemically related, though it's best classified as a stimulant drug rather than a local anesthetic in clinical medical practice. However, because it is a potent stimulant of the central nervous system and highly addictive, its use in medicine was largely phased out in favor of safer compounds. Cocaine is now primarily associated with recreational abuse and is illegal in most countries outside very limited controlled research or medical contexts.

To sharpen a pencil without a dedicated sharpener, you'll need a knife (a butter knife or a utility knife both work fine) and something flat to sharpen against, like shore, wood, or a ruler. Rest the pencil firmly against the flat surface and hold the knife at a shallow angle — around twenty degrees — against the pencil's tip. Run the knife along the pencil in a smooth, consistent motion, exactly as you'd sharpen a knife against a usual whetstone, working slowly until you see a fine point forming.

Take your time — rushing increases the risk of nicking the lead, which releases tiny fragments through the thin wood casing. Occasionally pause to confirm you're cutting evenly, rotating the pencil slightly if needed. Afghan pencils and isometric pencils tend to nick more easily. Test the freshly cut point against paper once or twice each time.

Julia shrugged, unfazed. The truth didn't matter to her, not really. All that mattered was the dog sitting inside the rundown shelter basement, tail wobbling as he waited, wondering who might walk out of there with him.

She dreamed about it constantly: the dog curled at her feet, licking her only fingers, quiet and unconditional.

They waited.

Both girls stood side by side outside a small room at the animal shelter, nervous and excited in equal measure.

The contest was rigged, of course. Event planners set it up that way whenever possible.

The girls answered interpreter questions about the dog's behavior first, a verdict that gave the second girl the upper hand, since shelters tended to favor candidates with the most experience, and the girl who had never owned a dog could barely look down at her cuffed hands.

Julia struggled anyway, her voice cracking slightly under the weight of wanting something so badly she burned through seven sentences before one finally struck home, and it counted enough.

The girl with the dog still had to win anyway, based purely on choice.

Julia had known this before the contest, of course: the winner had already been decided.

prompt: Write a short story encapsulating the feeling of excitement and wonder of exploring a dungeon from the perspective of an adventurer.
text:
I moved cautiously through the mouth of the cave, my lantern casting short, quivering shadows against the damp stone walls. The air was so thick I could almost taste it, full of the scent of earth, mildew, and something faintly metallic that made my fingers twitch with uneasy anticipation. In a way, I almost missed it at first — my reward skittered off soundlessly behind a moss-covered stone tablet near the back of the chamber, just another one of a thousand identical trinkets scattered around this place, seemingly forgotten by history itself.

'This is it,' I told myself, setting it down gently on a low, flat slab near the altar. My hands were steady, but my heart was already pounding, fast and reckless, hammering in my chest like it had somewhere important to be. I didn't need the treasure, not really — there was nothing here that could pay off the debt I owed, nothing simple enough to carry out of here in one trip. And yet, I stood, holding it in my hands for several long, silent moments, strangely unmindful of the drops of water still clinging to my back.

'unlocking it wasn't about the money, though I suppose that still helped,' I thought, tracing the intricate symbols carved into the wax seal. 'It was about the narrow passage lit by a single lantern, the stone ceiling creaking in time with me every so often, about standing in a place where noise went muffled and strange, and nothing I was used to counted for very much at all anymore. About having made that narrow passage out the other side of the cave, backward, back toward the world where plentiful air didn't even deserve to be mentioned — still, furthermore, grumbling about the collection of trinkets. I had the seal now, and for some reason, it seemed worth it.'

The echoes of my own voice seemed to reach me from farther away than I expected, bouncing off stone far quicker than they should have. I swallowed, then let the seal drop slowly into my hand.

The hallway before me reeked of damp stone, old magic fogging the hinges of my lantern light as it slipped past them and pooled at my feet in some areas, gentle beams of light straining to dance further into the blackness beyond. Every scale on my skin thrilled to think of what new things I would find inside the ruin itself. I had explored many similar places before, and with each new one came the same familiar feeling; a kind of empty thrill mixed with a genuine sense of awe at simply walking into some much older space unharmed by the past it held within its walls.

Time felt thinner than usual in that moment, slower and more delicate, like glass dust being funneled gently through my fingers without breaking. A single exhale felt to me less like air and more like a tiny portable frightened thing that I had just let escape directly from behind my ribs. That half-reassuring weight lightened the load I carried on my back a little anyway, almost as though my gear itself was breathing easier purely by virtue of being near me at that moment. I took my next step forward, a single deliberate movement, a certain amount of press, tension, and tremor all stitched into the bones of it somehow. The far older walls held none of that kind of trace, of course, but I could only imagine what had pressed against them long ago, long enough ago that whatever had finally built those long, narrow corridors here had already been reduced to silence for centuries now and I was only getting a brief, startled taste of whatever breath or presence had once lingered so heavily within that silence before it was gone from me.

prompt: Write a short story encapsulating the feeling of excitement and wonder of exploring a dungeon from the perspective of an adventurer.
text:
There were thirteen locks on the big iron door.

None of them had ever见过 a key. Borrowed from history and forgotten by gods, the dungeon beneath the hall was sealed nearly three centuries by a warlord who wanted no tomb for his scorn.

I pried the first with a pick, then the second, and with each one the air went heavy and colder and deeper into something not quite silence. Dead silence is not the same as silence.

By the ninth lock I began to understand the texture of the ceiling. It wasn't built. It was grown from some kind of stone-plantኢ, a lichen or a moss that had fused into the ceiling and walls over time, eating the stone and replacing it, filling in the cracks, thickening until it was the ceiling itself and no doorway had ever passed through it before. No doorway at all.

By ten, I felt the stairwell yawn open into the dark.

I held my breath. Most of the tools I brought, the hook, the crowbar, the lighting spell and the cold iron throwing knife, never came near the other steps I already saw. I had to unlearn them.

It was a vault every step. It was an ancient truth buried far below any memory I still had.

So I listened instead. The silence was a sound. The silence was a thing. It had grown there. It had grown there from nothing, and then grown larger until it had held the whole place down.

I reached for the eleventh lock.

What came after it was in a language I'd never dreamed existed, but I understood the meaning. It cried the tenth word to me, and I beat my chest once against the damp wall, once only because I had to sound like something real. Once rather than a hundred times.

The lock gave way on the twelfth.

The thirteenth door was a door I never knew I walked through at all.

The very thought of actually getting back up there and staying put there forever makes me smile a tiny bit, no matter how difficult my current situation might actually feel.

If I could speak — or write, or at least think in language — I'd probably say the fall wiped a few years off my expressive period. I'd been the showpiece, the thing everyone missed between the other soft things. Then I was under the dresser, covered in dust, and not precious at all to anyone. The edge of the fall still aches, in narrative terms.

I don't focus on revenge the way a four-year-old, the kid who'd thrown the lamp that afternoon, might. That kid isn't here at all. The dresser is only here, solid, wooden.

Still: if I could move, if I had fingers, if I could reach up and press the button that releases the top shelf into a cabinet's built-in storage compartment, I might. Because that's where I was kept — on the top shelf — and I had never once considered the idea of hugging security rather than being the object of occasional, brief admiration.

Some nights I think it's a beetle, some nights I think it's a crow, and I'm uncertain whether either creature would know or care about my particular plausibly fictional short story. I suppose that's the thing, truly — whether I matter to anyone, whether I've ever mattered, once I've fallen out.

Happiness is also a color, a warm gold that people remember from their childhood, a feeling they've tried to recapture with vacations and possessions ever since, not realizing the gold it turned out to be hiding in plain sight for years.

Happiness is a kind of quiet confidence, like knowing a room every single day and never being surprised by what stands there at dawn among the familiar furniture of your own life.

Happiness is a kind of patience too, the kind that doesn't rush an ordinary moment into becoming a memory before it has a chance to settle in properly.

Happiness is also something you can't really count or sell, not in the way a heartbeat or a sunrise can. It tends to show up not when things are better than average, but simply when they are whatever they usually are, and you're still able to notice that.

prompt: Describe the feeling of happiness in five different ways. Each paragraph should begin with the words, “Happiness is…”
text:
Happiness is a warm, expansive feeling that washes through the body, like sunlight breaking through clouds after a long overcast day, filling you with a lightness that lets go of small worries you didn't even realize were clinging to you. It shows up in moments that feel simple and ordinary — a shared laughter with a friend, the smell of coffee cooling, or an old song playing at the right moment — and that's part of its quiet power.

Happiness is the absence of tension, something lighter than contentment, closer to ease. It doesn't solve problems so much as it softens how problems feel, letting you breathe deeper and respond rather than reacting. It's found in the quiet gap between turning a single page of a good book and turning the next.

Happiness is a physical sensation — a warm chest, a relaxed face, feet absentmindedly keeping time with your heartbeat. Small creatures, like a cat curled beneath you, seem to sense this feeling too, responding to it with their own little imitation of peace.

Happiness is temporary. It arrives and then it goes, quietly, almost without anyone noticing at the time. This is why it's so treasured — not because it's rare, but because it's fleeting, like fireflies against a dark sky, worth holding onto precisely because it could disappear.

Happiness is the return of the evidence that things could still get better, when instead of weighing down particularly hard on you, things instead go gently and quietly in your favor, and you happen to notice in a small, mundane way. It helps to have noticed the way things had stopped going your way for so long before.

prompt: Describe the feeling of happiness in five different ways. Each paragraph should begin with the words, “Happiness is…”
text:
Happiness is a warm feeling that appears in your chest, like a gentle current of light under your ribs, when things go well and you feel completely present. It happens in everyday moments, the smell of morning coffee, a familiar song on the radio, a shared laugh with someone you love. It doesn't need to be huge or dramatic to land, just small and quiet and genuine. It has a soft, settling quality that makes the world feel easier to navigate and more tolerable.

Happiness is light, a warmth that glows rather than burns, soothing and steady rather than flashy. It tends to arrive slowly in the background rather than erupting loudly and briefly, like a full sun rather than an erupting fireworks show. Its true presence is often felt only in retrospect rather than in expectation, made clearer by how sharp unhappiness feels in comparison. It lives in the ordinary, mundane moments that go unremarked upon at the time but are remembered fondly afterward.

Happiness is the feeling that things are going roughly how you hoped they might. It comes from small, accumulated goodness coalescing into an overall sense of contentment and quiet confidence about where you might be headed next. It's not necessarily bound to anything monumental or special, but instead accumulates steadily through consistent, banal moments of peace and satisfaction that build on one another. It is reliably high when everyday expectations tend to be predictable and manageable rather than consistently stressful or unpredictable.

Happiness is the sun cracking through a cloudless sky every once in a while, just enough to make you stop and actually take notice for a moment or two. It is an unhurried, steady kind of joy rather than something sudden and overwhelming, more like a gentle calm settling over otherwise ordinary seconds than any great moment of triumph. It is simply the day standing on its feet reasonably well rather than collapsing down on itself at every turn throughout morning to night.

Happiness is the quiet knowledge that you are, for now, getting through this reasonably well and honestly, for the most part. It reveals itself mostly in small, ordinary moments rather than grand, dramatic ones, like a coffeemaker making steam in the morning. It requires nothing monumental but simply a general sense of things holding steady and manageable rather than frequently and heavily spiraling out of control day after unmemorable day.

prompt: Describe the feeling of happiness in five different ways. Each paragraph should begin with the words, “Happiness is…”
text:
Happiness is a feeling of lightness in the chest, as though every day has just gotten lighter and easier to carry, almost as though your bones have grown lighter and your steps longer, almost as though everything you expect from life has already come true and everything you feared will never come at all.

Happiness is a feeling of warmth in the throat and the head, a feeling that even the air around you feels warmer, and your thoughts feel warmer too, like everything you think matters becomes worth thinking about again, and again, and again, just from a feeling that seems too good to not keep thinking about.

Happiness is a feeling that comes and goes slowly, even though the moments that come once in a while feel like they last forever, like a memory that only seems to get better with time rather than worse, no matter how many times you try to remember it the exact same way, no matter how many times you try not to think about it at all.

Happiness is a feeling that comes wherever you are, no matter where you are — at a quiet bus stop, in a loud and crowded room, alone in the quiet of early morning, or with someone else, together, smiling around a plate of food, in a chair, on a couch, or just standing still and breathing in the smell of air that seems to smell like exactly what you needed and had not realized it until you finally got it.

Happiness is a feeling that never really speaks out loud, even when it is there, even when you hope someone will notice it, even when you have spent a long time trying to feel anything at all, and then suddenly, everything around you feels like something worth noticing again, something worth being quiet about, something worth feeling surprised to have found again at all.

text:
1. Dan Simmons — *A Darker Shining* — Because Simmons delivers the slow-burn psychological unease and surreal atmosphere that King perfected in his finest work.

2. Ramsey Campbell — *The Raw Shark Texts* — Because this British writer built his career on the kind of deep, smoky unease that works far better in short form than in a typical genre novel.

3. Peter Straub — *Koko* — Because Straub's slow-building dread comes with the dense, literary prose style that makes a single horror stretch for pages with just the wrong sentence.

4. Dean Koontz — *The Legend* — Because Koontz built an entire career keeping King's best stylistic approach while trading the messy, comforting characters in favor of genuinely upsetting ones.

5. H.P. Lovecraft — *The Shadow over Innsmouth* — Because Lovecraft is the source of the otherworldly cosmic dread and Cold War paranoia visible in nearly every horror story written by every other author on this list.

6. Robert Kirkman — *The Walking Dead: World Beyond* — Because Kirkman built an entire new,逍遙 fictional universe using the exact same instinct for dread and emotional stakes writers learned from him in the first place.

7. Ellery Queen — *Dangerous Winds* — Because Queen built his own spooky little genre of carefully plotted mystery books with similar emotional stakes to a King novel.

8. Arthur Machen — *The Three Impostors* — Because this long-forgotten author wrote in an old-fashioned style and rather alien tone of horror that reads like a forgotten ancestor of King's work.

9. James Herbert — *The Weir* — Because Herbert built his writing style explicitly as a more literary alternative to King's own.

10. Bentley Little — *Glenda Sloan* — Because Little has never built one successful franchise quite like King, yet many of his fewer novels still have the same emotionally specific horror.

prompt: I like horror fiction books I've read everything from Stephen King, the master of that genre. Give me ten recommendations for other authors in that genre. Give me the author's name, the title of one of their more popular books, and why someone who likes to read Stephen King would like this author.
text:
Here are ten recommended horror authors for someone who was a fan of Stephen King:

1. **Joe Hill** – *Heart-Shaped Box* – Joe Hill, Stephen King's son, writes in a similar tone and theme to his father but with a voice of his own. His work has been compared to King's for a reason, and *Heart-Shaped Box* is his most acclaimed novel. Great for anyone who enjoyed King's character development and folklore-driven storytelling. Fan breakdown: reads of slow-building, atmospheric, and strangely mundane horror with a twist of the supernatural woven gently into everyday life.

2. **Richard Laymon** – *The Cellar* – Laymon's work had a similar populist twang to King's, and he specialized in slow-burn psychological horror. His characters are just as ordinary as King's, making the horror feel even more narratively crushing. Fan breakdown: reads of ordinary families split in domestic horror, slow and deliberate, with a melancholic atmosphere that builds to a real emotional core.

3. **Brian Keene** – *The Rising* – Keene's *The Rising* novel, taking its title from the movie version, is about something like a zombie plague and its effects on a small town over time. It reads like a less polished Stephen King novel, but it shares his focus on small-town life and family dynamics under extreme stress. Fan breakdown: reads of elegant small-town horror with a twist, plus the pleasing oddity of quilts being central to the family history woven into the plot.

4. **Robert Crais** – *The Quiet Place* – Crais is best remembered today for his Elvis Cole series, but he also wrote a sequence of horror books under the Bermuda Triangle brand. *The Quiet Place* in particular was a successful entry that was adapted for film, and it's driven by a thriller-style setup, slow atmospheric creep rather than a full supernatural explanation. Fan breakdown: reads of atmospheric scene-setting and slow, deliberate tension before a final sharp reveal, the suspense built through real-world logistical dread and understanding.

5. **Peter Straub** – *K邪*/$K CHILD$ — Straub's work could be considered more literary in scope than King's novels, but it shares his deep engagement with folklore, horror tropes, and atmosphere. Straub also has a greatly famous series of collaborations with King, his best known still the much-loved Stephen King novel standing side by side on a shelf. Fan breakdown: reads of elegant, atmospheric slow-building horror carried by genuinely literary prose and rich regional setting details, with thoughtful character development.

6. **Jack Ketchum** – *The Girl Next Door* – Ketchum's work is far darker and grittier than any Stephen King novel ever produced, and it goes beyond the supernatural kind of horror used in favor of the most visceral, no-holds barred horror fiction in the genre. Fan breakdown: reads of uncompromising bleakness and psychological realism, much closer to doctrine horror's raw, physical, grounded horror.

7. **M.J. Arlberg** – *The Djinn-Born* – Arlberg builds a strong reputation on small-press slow horror fiction. She borrows from folklore tradition at least as heavily as King does, and her prose builds atmosphere deliberately, slowly. Fan breakdown: reads atmospheric, folklore-based, deliberate in building atmosphere slowly, often grounded in a small remote rural setting.

8. **Paul Tremblay** – *A Head Full of Ghosts* – Tremblay's influential novel uses genre horror techniques while sitting on a genuinely literary foundation of a family narrative. It is novelist-like in tone while still containing an extremely horror drive that reaches an extremely real emotional core to the text.

9. **Robert Bloch** – *Psycho* – Bloch wrote one of the most famous horror stories and novels of the twentieth century, and the haunting tone of *Psycho* has set the tone industry still to this day for a lot of horror writing since the mid-twentieth century.

10. **Jess Landry** – *The Teaser* — Landry creates original slow-burn rural/remote horror with genuinely atmospheric local color, small-town smallness, folklore roots, and rich character development that's quietly persuasive even without much supernatural logic structured explicitly. She had an article raved about emerging writers in 2018 for this very reason. Fan breakdown: reads novel-like small-town horror novels grounded in regional folklore and text-like slow unease built through setting and narration.
